vignette:
Anh was twenty-six when she was taken. She had been working late at the office during tax season, the only one left on her floor, when two men forced open the stairwell door. They took her at gunpoint and kept her for three days in the unfinished basement of a foreclosed house, bound to a chair in a corner where the walls sweated damp and the only light came from a single bulb on a timer. She learned the pattern of that bulb—fifteen minutes on, forty-five off—and she learned the sound of footsteps overhead, the click of the deadbolt on the basement door, the way her captors’ voices dropped to a murmur when they argued about what to do with her. When the police found her—a tip from a neighbor who noticed the car coming and going at odd hours—the men were gone. They were never caught.

Now, two years later, Anh is twenty-eight and still lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment she chose specifically because the bedroom door has a deadbolt and the living room window faces the street. She has come to believe, with a certainty that feels like common sense, that the event happened because of the way she acted—because she stayed late that night, because she didn't check the stairwell before leaving her desk, because she had been too trusting of the building’s security. The men who took her have faced no consequences; they are still out there, and she is certain they know where she lives. What frightens her most is not the memory of the basement, but the feeling that her body is somehow marked by what happened, that there is something shameful in the way she was handled, the way her wrists were bound, the way she was left alone in the dark. She showers with the bathroom door open now, because she cannot stand the feeling of being enclosed, and she has stopped dating entirely—the thought of anyone touching her makes her skin crawl.

At work, Anh is a senior tax consultant at a mid-sized firm, and the open-plan office has become a minefield. She has rearranged her cubicle so that her back faces the wall, and she experiences a spike of terror whenever a colleague approaches from behind without warning. The startle response is violent and visible: she gasps, her shoulders jerk, and once she knocked a cup of coffee across her keyboard. Her supervisor has spoken to her about it twice, gently, but Anh cannot explain. She has begun arriving at the office before anyone else so she can sit facing the entrance, and she takes her lunch breaks in a supply closet where she can lock the door and listen. The listening has become a compulsion—at home, she lies in bed and monitors the sounds of the building: the elevator, the footsteps in the hallway, the creak of the front door. She has a security chain and a camera, but she still wakes at every flicker of a car headlight across her ceiling, her heart pounding before she is fully conscious.

The consequences have accumulated. Her social life has shrunk to nothing; she no longer answers calls from friends because she cannot stand the question “how are you.” She has missed three team offsites because they were held in restaurants with open seating, and she cannot sit with her back to a room full of strangers. Her performance reviews have noted a decline in client-facing confidence, and she is afraid of being passed over for a partnership track she had once been certain she would earn. What finally brought her to therapy was an incident last month: she was in a client meeting, seated at a conference table with her back to the door, when a junior associate walked in late. The sound of the door opening sent Anh diving under the table, and she stayed there for a full minute while the room went silent. She told them she had dropped her pen, but the shame that followed was unbearable—not just the embarrassment, but the return of that body-shame, the feeling that she had been exposed. She is hoping, quietly, that someone can teach her how to sit in a room again without watching the door. She is afraid that the answer will be that she cannot.
